⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An MRI scan of the basal ganglia, seen here in section and colour-coded.Credit: Zephyr/SPL.
  • Recent findings suggest that the basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information.
  • Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An MRI scan of the basal ganglia, seen here in section and colour-coded.Credit: Zephyr/SPL.

Recent findings suggest that the basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information. They are linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions from Parkinson’s and Huntington’s disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction.

Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is described in a collection of 26 papers published in Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron. The research includes understudied neurons1, provides insights about how some brain cells change with age2 and suggests which might be linked to diseases3.

The atlas, a collaboration between hundreds of scientists in nine countries, is part of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) — a US$500-million project launched in 2022 by the US National Institutes of Health aimed at creating reference maps of mammalian brains.

“It’s a massive dictionary that we needed in the field,” says Ana Muñoz-Manchado, a neuroscientist at the University of Cádiz in Spain, who studies the basal ganglia in neurodegenerative disorders.

The basal ganglia atlas contains 21 million cells from the brains of six humans, three million cells from three rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, and 1.5 million cells from two marmosets4. The researchers also used data from previously published maps of the whole mouse brain5,6.

By comparing the basal ganglia between the primate species, the researchers identified 61 cell types in humans, macaques and marmosets that have been conserved over 76 million years3.

The team analysed brain tissue samples from different developmental stages across the lifespan of the species. The latest work combines information about these cells in unprecedented detail, from measurements of their gene expression and DNA modifications that control gene regulation to recordings of their electrical activity, as well as how DNA is folded inside their nuclei.

The researchers also mapped where each cell is located in the brain and designed a common framework to characterize and annotate the cells. It is “essentially a scaffold on which we can now fairly readily complete the rest of the brain”, explains Michael Hawrylycz, a bioinformatician at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who took part in the project.

One study examined 1.1 million cells in the basal ganglia’s largest structure — known as the striatum — from 19 deceased human donors7. Unlike many other brain areas, the striatum has no neat anatomical boundaries. The researchers identified six zones in the human and macaque striatum that had distinct molecular signatures, each containing distinct populations of neurons and glial cells.

“The cells in these zones all look the same under the microscope, but have very strong transcriptional differences and are strikingly consistent from person to person,” said co-author Evan Macosko, a neurobiologist at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in a press release from the institute.

Macosko and his colleagues also found that gene expression patterns that distinguished each zone from the other became increasingly similar with age, particularly in brain regions affected by Huntington’s or Parkinson’s disease.

Another study analysed nearly four million cells in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from 178 deceased adult donors aged from 27 to more than 902. The researchers found that the cellular make-up of the two brain regions varied between people, particularly for non-neuronal cells known as glial cells. This underscores the need for brain cell atlases to account for these individual differences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Milan are prepared to offer €60m plus add-ons to buy Brazil talent Endrick from Real Madrid in January, claim Italian reports, with one very crucial advantage over Roma and Arsenal.

It is no secret that these three clubs are interested in picking up Endrick during the January transfer window, as the 20-year-old is frustrated at the lack of regular playing time for the Merengues.

Jose Mourinho is adamant that the youngster should not leave, but considering the loan experience at Olympique Lyonnais last season, the decision might be beyond him.

According to the Corriere dello Sport, there are two elements that put Milan at the very top of the list for the striker.

The first is that while Roma and perhaps Arsenal are only prepared to offer a loan, the Rossoneri can put €60m on the table to purchase Endrick outright, and could add some bonuses on top worth another €10m.

This could even be negotiated to give Real Madrid a buy-back clause set at €80m, giving them the option of controlling his future.

The other substantial element in this deal is the fact Endrick’s agency is Roc Nation.

Their ties go very deep indeed with Milan, because the fresh CEO of Milan Sports and Entertainment is Brett Yormark, whose twin brother Michael is President of Roc Nation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026.

The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning. ‘Fin a la racha,’ the headline remarked. The end of the run.

For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.

In a recent development, for England, the feeling was very different. Because Sunday night in the cauldron of the Metropolitano felt very much like a beginning. Thomas Tuchel has been the head coach for almost two years but this was the moment of his true arrival.

This was the victory that freed us from looking back to the Groundhog Day pain of that World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in Atlanta last summer and allowed us to look forward to a future that seems luminous and full of hope.

Recent findings suggest that this was the victory that allowed us to stop blaming Tuchel for what happened four months ago and start looking forwards again, dreaming about the glories that he might yet deliver. This was the victory that validated Tuchel and why the FA hired him in the first place. This was the victory that allowed us to believe he might be the Messiah after all.

This felt like the moment when he embraced us, with all our quirks and football idiosyncrasies, and we embraced him. He had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it with bells on. Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game and welded it to his principles and the result is intoxicating.

Thomas Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game to down world champions Spain.

Industry observers note that once you have seen England play the way they did for an hour against Spain, you are lost. You are lost to the belief that the 62 years of hurt might really be coming to an end at Wembley in the final of the European Championship in the summer of 2028. You are lost to the idea that, finally, everything is falling into place.

For the 63 minutes up until the sending off of Elliot Anderson, I have never seen an England performance as good as the one that unfolded in the Metropolitano. Spain are the best team in the world and England outclassed them and stupefied them. They were better than them with the ball and better than them without the ball. They were magnificent.

Because of the context, because of the wonder of the stage, because of the odds they faced, England’s victory over Mexico in the grandeur and the mayhem of the mighty Azteca Stadium during the World Cup might edge Sunday’s performance but for pure football, what England delivered in Madrid demands comparison with the best they have played for many a year.

Sources indicate that this year’s World Cup came just too soon but now Tuchel and England understand each other perfectly. And now England are purring. They have a manager who commands the players’ respect and they have a group of players that commands the respect of the manager.

It has been revealed that yes, it was just a Nations League group game but it was against one of the best national sides the world has ever seen. England worked so ferociously and attacked so fluently and defended so devotedly that they reached a level that drew admiration even from their opponents.

Recent findings suggest that many, many things will live long in the memory. James Trafford’s miraculous double save in the dying minutes gets better every time I watch it. Ben White’s goal channels the beauty of Carlos Alberto’s strike for Brazil against Italy in the 1970 World Cup Final, too. Let’s hope that strike, and his superb defensive performance, bring an end to the boos that have been his companion of late.

Jude Bellingham was relentless, tireless and glided through the game against Spain.

Tuchel had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it.

In a recent development, and then there was Jude Bellingham. Just when you think you can’t admire him any more than you do, he delivers a performance like the one he produced against Spain, a performance that lifted him above even the exalted organization of the other players on two fine teams.

Bellingham was tireless. He was relentless. He glided past challenges. He thundered into tackles. He dominated midfield. He has the heart and the sheer brilliant indomitability that Bryan Robson possessed.

In a recent development, bellingham has it in him to be England’s greatest ever player. He needs trophies to fulfil that destiny but maybe, finally, trophies are in reach again.

He has the team around him to do it, which Robson never quite had. Jordan Pickford is a good goalkeeper but Trafford might just be better. Ezri Konsa had his best game for England in Spain. White and Lewis Hall were superb at full back. Little more needs to be remarked about England’s front six. They are as good as any unit in world football.

Harry Kane, of course, was the best player in the world last year. Some seem to assume that the Ballon d’Or will inevitably pass to Yamal or Kylian Mbappe next. I think it is more likely to be Bellingham.

The man is a colossus. He is a footballer who has everything. He does not know how to be beaten.

Bellingham saw off Barcelona rival Lamine Yamal - and could beat him to the Ballon d'Or.

Recent findings suggest that with them together, the sky is the limit. And Bellingham has also proved to be a player of immense mental strength. It was not so long ago that people worried about his discipline but the fortitude he showed when he was being targeted by Argentina at the World Cup was the best answer to that.

In a recent development, he and Kane are England’s axis of ambition on the pitch. Tuchel is lucky to have them and they are lucky to have him, too. The coach has reached the point where his tactics and his team-building are bearing fruit.

Now England have a team-manager package that genuinely need fear nobody. The victory against Spain was a rehearsal for the bigger stage of major tournaments. Going down to 10 men after 63 minutes against the best team in the world might not have been in the script but that is what rehearsals are for.

After Sunday night in the Metropolitano, England are ready for their close-up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

It has been revealed that eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”.

In a recent development, this was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

Industry observers note that you should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and mentioned “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM.

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

Industry observers note that so while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

Industry observers note that the anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

It has been revealed that arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”.

It has been revealed that they were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

According to recent reports, it was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Sources indicate that FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL.

Recent findings suggest that as the home fans set off flares, filling the air with plumes of thick, red smoke, the theme tune to Captain Pugwash was played. Arteta tried to find answers from his coaching staff, amid the cacophony, but occasionally you do not have to look too deep for answers.

According to recent reports, could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

In a recent development, so it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Recent findings suggest that A game of attack against defence played out for the remainder before Dowman was harshly dismissed in the 85th minute after reacting to a tough challenge from Neal. There was still time for Fleetwood’s Lynch to make two excellent saves from White and Odegaard in added time as Arsenal tried to avoid the shoot-out lottery. They could not and how it hurt them.

According to recent reports, HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ.

Recent findings suggest that “Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and removed,” Matt Lawlor, the Fleetwood manager, noted. “To me, there was that feeling we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special.

According to recent reports, “To be giving that to football fans and especially Fleetwood fans is unbelievably special. I’m really proud of it. Football’s a funny old game, isn’t it?”.

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players. I haven’t seen anyone not doing what is required at this level. But, obviously, we insisted so much, we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, obviously, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t. And football is about that.

According to recent reports, attitude wise, absolutely zero [wrong] otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way. It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline.

Something that we discussed already before the match.

It’s difficult to see on the cameras, I prefer to watch it back properly and I will assess the situation.

We will learn from everything [on if he will learn from it].

In a recent development, I don’t think it will [sink in], it’s really hard to address the players when we have a league game on Saturday and I didn’t want to be the bearer of reality. The biggest night in the club’s history. We’ve beaten the champions, somehow!

According to recent reports, we knew before the game, we’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to go to the best team in the country and the most organised team in the country and the best of the basics and the world-class players, in that we’re going to go and outplay them. So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them. And I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.

Obviously, the goal happens, but they’re going to happen; they’re so good at football. The footballers that they have, the gaps that they find and we see it every week in the Premier League.

To beat the English champions on penalties, credit to everyone one of these lads. We looked at Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We compared it even though these are the champions. We thought ‘if we lay it all out there, let’s see what happens.

Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Eberechi Eze are among the players stepping off the bus, so at the very least it will be a strong bench.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

There is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

Sources indicate that “We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”.

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta noted: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock.
  • In a recent development, epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared.
  • In a recent development, it is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was confirmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock.

In a recent development, epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

In a recent development, it is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was confirmed. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so rapidly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” indicates Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

Ronaldo's decision follows a rift with the current head coach Jorge Jesus. Last month, the striker left Portugal's training camp aboard his private jet following a disagreement with the coach, followed by an open letter and apologies to the fans and the team where he explained his decision, without mentioning the manager. The Portuguese federation later suspended the player for 30 days but he was eligible to be called for the upcoming games against Denmark and Wales.

Ronaldo posted a video message on his social media announcing his decision to retire from the national team: "To the Portuguese people, the day has come to hand back the number seven shirt of the national team that belongs to us all. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the time has come to hand it over to the future. It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made solely with the head; they are also made with the heart.".

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner played his sixth and last World Cup this summer in the United States, Canada and Mexico, when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the round of 16 of the tournament.

Industry observers note that "A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever is coming to an end. When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer. I see millions of Portuguese people whom I've never met in person, but who have been part of my life. Because, at the end of the day, football is so much more than just a game. Football is about the people. Throughout my entire career with the national team, I've strived to push my limits. I wanted to win, I wanted to be the best, I wanted to make history," he said.

In a recent development, "I've always been hard on myself. I've always wanted more; I've always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt. There were perfect afternoons and evenings; there were victories I'll never forget. There were defeats that I still find hard to recall today. I also failed, I also suffered, and there were moments when I wasn't able to give the Portuguese people what they so desperately wanted. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal. Over the years, I've learnt some very simple things. Goals come and go, trophies end up in museums, and records are eventually broken. But there is one thing that time can never erase: the place we hold in people's hearts. If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget your worries, and feel nothing but pride in our country, then it was all worth it. Because that's what being Portuguese is all about. We suffer together, we rise together. No captain walks alone and you're all part of my story. Portugal will always need young people who dream, players who never give up, latest generations who believe it's possible to reach places no one has reached before. Because a country that continues to create new heroes is a country that never stops believing in itself.".

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Industry observers note that liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

Industry observers note that “There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola mentioned ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Barcelona remain admirers of Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol, but the Catalan giants appear to accept that signing him is unrealistic under their current financial conditions.
  • Hansi Flick wants to strengthen the left side of his defence, and Gvardiol is an obvious fit because of his ability to operate both as a centre-back and left-back.
  • However, Man City have no intention of losing one of their most notable defenders, while Barcelona’s limited spending power makes any major deal particularly difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barcelona remain admirers of Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol, but the Catalan giants appear to accept that signing him is unrealistic under their current financial conditions.

Hansi Flick wants to strengthen the left side of his defence, and Gvardiol is an obvious fit because of his ability to operate both as a centre-back and left-back.

However, Man City have no intention of losing one of their most notable defenders, while Barcelona’s limited spending power makes any major deal particularly difficult.

According to AS, Barcelona have asked about Gvardiol and continue to rate him highly, but a move currently “seems impossible”.

According to recent reports, the 24-year-old signed a fresh Man City contract earlier this year that runs until 2031, strengthening the club’s position considerably. City also rejected Barcelona’s enquiry during negotiations involving Rodri last summer, making it clear that Gvardiol was not available.

City Xtra’s report on Barcelona’s enquiry explains that Barcelona raised Gvardiol’s name during discussions with City, but the Premier League side had no interest in opening negotiations.

Gvardiol’s versatility is one of the main reasons Barcelona remain interested. Flick wants a left-footed defender capable of contributing in possession, but other targets such as Alessandro Bastoni are also considered financially difficult.

From City’s perspective, there is very little reason to entertain Barcelona’s interest.

Gvardiol is entering his prime, has become one of Enzo Maresca’s most trusted defenders and is tied down for several years. Replacing a player who can perform equally well at centre-back and left-back would also be expensive.

A CaughtOffside report previously confirmed Barcelona’s interest but also noted that City were unwilling to sell and that Gvardiol himself had shown no desire to force an exit.

In a recent development, that is the key point. Barcelona may admire him, but admiration alone does not create a realistic transfer opportunity.

Their financial limitations remain the biggest obstacle, while City have both contractual control and sporting reasons to keep him.

Unless Gvardiol’s own stance changes dramatically or Barcelona generate significant funds through player sales, this looks more like a long-term ambition than a genuine January possibility.

For now, City can afford to be completely relaxed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was born in North Wales in 1980, and my first memory of football was playing for the school team as a kid.

As a nine or 10-year-old I started getting my cousin’s hand-me-down Everton shirts, and this certainly helped me decide which of the local sides I was going to follow!

The two red sides close by (Wrexham and the other lot) never once turned my head.

Sources indicate that and then, in 1991, my mind was made up for good. My uncle asked me if I’d like to go to watch Everton play.

It was the first ever game I’d been to watch live. It was at Bramall Lane, and I’ll never ever forget it.

My uncle got us to the ground early and took me and my cousin to wait for the players’ coach to turn up.

The coach arrived and as I was only a little kid at that point, my uncle lifted me up to get a glimpse of the players.

Industry observers note that the first player I saw was substantial Neville Southall and I reached over to pat him on the back and wish him good luck. He glanced over his shoulder and gave me a wry smile.

Not only was I now hooked on Everton, but all I wanted to be from that point on was a goalkeeper.

In a recent development, A few years later I got to taste my first ever trophy win as an Evertonian. Me and my dad watched the whole FA Cup final build-up from Grandstand in the morning to Match of the Day, with the game in between.

We couldn’t get tickets to the final, but my uncle and cousin did go the Charity Shield.

Even though that was my last taste of silverware as an Evertonian, my love for this club has never wavered.

I’m now 46 years old, lived in Australia for 20 years and I’m happily married with seven children – six of which have all been to Goodison and the youngest has beat me to visit the upcoming stadium last year!

My highlights of the last 35 years are:.

-              - My first game in 1991.

-              - 1995 and the FA Cup victory.

-              - Going to Howard’s testimonial a few months before leaving for Australia.

-              - Spending a day painting parts of Goodison in 2013.

-              - Goodison trips with my dad, cousins, uncle and taking my six kids to see the eventual champions in 2016.

-              -Taking my two sons to the games in Sydney.

-              - My daughter (who now lives in Rochdale) going to the last game at Goodison.

-              - And my wife taking our two youngest daughters to see our stone at the new ground last year.

I’ve got so many fond memories of our beautiful club, and I can’t wait to make millions more in the coming decades.

There is no other football club for me or my family. Once a Blue, always a Blue.

That is ultimately an improvement for Tottenham when you consider that they finished 17th in the past two top flight campaigns, including only escaping relegation to the Championship on the final day of last season.

Despite the summer spend, there is a feeling that the north London outfit are still lacking in the centre-forward position, with that being one of the positions that the club didn't significantly strengthen in the summer.

De Zerbi had Richarlison, Dominic Solanke and Will Lankshear available to him going into the summer window, but the former informed the Italian coach that he wanted to leave and fell out of favour, while Solanke is struggling to find the goalscoring form that would be expected from a £60m player.

Tottenham also decided to cash in on Lankshear after Championship side Middlesbrough arrived with an offer worth £10m, plus £10m if they win promotion to the Premier League, and it might be a decision they already have some regrets about, despite the money brought in for an academy graduate who only made six first-team appearances.

According to the Sun, Spurs are already keeping an eye on Lankshear's performances for Boro this term, with the player beginning the campaign by scoring 15 goals in 16 games in all competitions for the Teesside outfit.

The Championship high-flyers are remarked to be ready to demand £70m already if any Premier League club comes calling in January, as they look to secure promotion to the Premier League.

While Lankshear has the attributes to become a top Premier League striker, Tottenham should forget about him and move for Junior Kroupi instead.

De Zerbi has used Omar Marmoush in the centre-forward role this season at times when Dominic Solanke hasn't started, although it is another experiment that has so far failed to work out with the Egyptian yet to show that clinical instinct in front of goal.

TEAMtalk reported earlier this month that Spurs are keen on France international Junior Kroupi, and are even ready to offer players to Bournemouth in exchange in order to get a head-start on their Premier League rivals for a deal.

There is a common feeling that the 20-year-old may have been on the move in the summer had he not suffered an injury, and he has only just returned from that problem, scoring his first goal for his nation during the current international break.

It is the latest milestone in a rapid rise for the forward, who was in stunning form in his first season in English football last term, scoring the most goals in a season for any teenager in Premier League history.

Junior Kroupi has a huge future ahead of him if he continues his meteoric rise, and it would be no surprise if he becomes the next big-money transfer away from Bournemouth in the not-too-distant future.

The 20-year-old has already been labelled as 'generational' and 'world-class' by teammate Marcus Tavernier, and the fact he is already playing under Zinedine Zidane for the senior France side says it all.

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

In a recent development, had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

In a recent development, what a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the problems Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

According to recent reports, thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major glitch for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a major day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

According to recent reports, “We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

In a recent development, it might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

Recent findings suggest that james Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

Sources indicate that the roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

In a recent development, hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

According to recent reports, it must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

Recent findings suggest that the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 14:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:35 EST, 16 November 2026.

Sources indicate that 'It was like meeting a kid at a sixth-form careers day'. That was the verdict, slightly unflattering but endearing all the same, of one Premier League chief after encountering James Trafford.

When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.

He is the son of a Cumbrian farmer and the Lego was of a tractor, which he would save for later in the tournament. 'You don't want to go too early,' he noted.

None of this is a criticism. Far from it. There was a boyish charm, an innocence, even, and Trafford was engaging firm. Nonetheless, he did not sound ready for the likes of a World Cup semi-final against Argentina. Thomas Tuchel agreed.

Industry observers note that but every boy will one day become a man. On a ferocious and febrile night in Madrid, no place for adolescents, we may just have witnessed James Trafford's graduation ceremony.

Without his double save in stoppage-time, England would have left Spain without a famous, and deserved, victory. One Spanish title labelled it 'la actuacion de su vida', the performance of his life. You wonder how much they saw of his loan spell at Accrington Stanley, but the sentiment stands.

James Trafford celebrates with Jarell Quansah, Dan Burn and Ezri Konsa during his starring performance in Spain.

Trafford pictured with his farmer father, David, in the cab of his tractor with their dogs (Source: James Trafford).

Madrid daily AS exclaimed: 'Magisterio de Trafford!' Translated, 'A Trafford Masterclass!'. They claim he was the reason Spain could not complete their comeback, and they would be right.

When Tuchel stood with us in a corridor of the Metropolitano Stadium on the eve of the game, he had no issue confirming that Trafford would start. His message, though, was clear - it was sink or swim for a goalkeeper who turned 24 last month.

Recent findings suggest that not only did Trafford keep his head above water, it was he who pulled the team ashore. It was he to whom his senior colleagues ran in celebration. Ezri Konsa nearly took the shirt off Trafford's back, such was the force of his gratitude. But maybe this was the occasion when Trafford took the No 1 jersey from the back of Jordan Pickford, the holder for nearly a decade.

Recent findings suggest that pickford has done nothing wrong. Were Trafford to still display that maturity deficit, Pickford would be a reliable custodian heading to Euro 2028. This is not Peter Shilton post Italia 90, an uncomfortable truth of a great in need of the retirement barn. The 32-year-old has plenty to give on the back of all he has already given.

This, admitted Tuchel after the 3-2 win, is a selection dilemma that allows a manager to sleep well at night.

'There is no headache at all!' he boomed. 'I'm so far away from a headache, I cannot imagine.

Trafford left Manchester City with the initiative to usurp Jordan Pickford as England No 1.

Jude Bellingham certainly seemed impressed with the performance of the goalkeeper.

According to recent reports, 'This is what we wanted. This is the best thing that can happen to all of us, also to Pickers. It is amazing how they push each other, and if then Traff has a performance like this, he has it because he knows he's well prepared. He gets the push from his colleagues and competitors.'.

Tuchel has seen enough of Trafford in training and around camp to believe he is ready for promotion. He has watched him for Leeds, where he rates as the best performing goalkeeper in the Premier League. His 'net goals prevented' (4.4) and 'save percentage' (81.4) are higher than any rival this season, including Pickford.

In a recent development, 'You always have to deserve your place,' added Tuchel. 'You will never get a gift and just get a game (for the sake of it). So he deserved to play and we expected this kind of performance. It was not only the last save, but also the build-up play and not losing focus. He has proved it on this stage, so this gives him a lot of belief. Now, it's on him to keep going for it.'.

It, you presume, is the No 1 jersey. Trafford has made no secret of his desire to take it from Pickford, and he told us in the summer that such ambition was the motivation behind him wanting to leave Manchester City for a second time.

That day, he flipped his room key with a magician's sleight of hand throughout the interview, a dexterity useful for Lego. Better still for fingertip saves such as the one to deny Aymeric Laporte in the 91st minute.

Sources indicate that also in the gift pack from his girlfriend were two face masks. 'Very thoughtful,' he quipped. But that is another observation, bordering on concern, that some prospective buyers have made in recent years - on the goalkeeping scale of uber professional to joker, he resides too close to the latter. We have seen, even this season, the odd concentration lapse that speaks to that thought.

Trafford has played a starring role in goal since moving to Leeds United in the summer.

Sources indicate that but there was also a feeling that Trafford needed more exposure and responsibility before the penny dropped and his value was realised. Already, £95million has been spent on him in transfer fees.

At Leeds, and now with England, he has been given that stage, as Tuchel calls it. The head coach maintains that Pickford is his first choice, but it was Trafford he picked for both Nations League fixtures against Spain, the ones that really mattered, the ones that would strengthen or threaten his own employment.

As for Trafford's career prospects, to revisit our opening line, England's No 1 sounds like a fair vocation.

Thomas Tuchel wants England to use victory in the Nations League finals as a springboard to winning Euro 2028 at Wembley.

The head coach admits it has taken him a while to recover from the trauma of his side’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July, for which he was heavily criticised.

But after beating world champions Spain 3-2 on Sunday night, topping their Nations League group ahead of March’s quarter-finals and next summer's finals, Tuchel is finally able to look forward with positivity and belief.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I saw the celebrations in Portugal when they won the Nations League,’ he said. ‘It’s just the best, the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves and to gain confidence, to see where we are and to adjust our game where we need to, that’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it.’.

Sources indicate that england have won five of their six matches since the World Cup, losing only to Spain at Wembley in September. In the build up to that game, Tuchel was involved in heated exchanges with observers who continued to question his tactics in the final half hour against Argentina.

’It took me a while to digest (the World Cup exit) and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together,’ he said.

Sources indicate that ‘We had reviews and so on, but clarity then came together with the players. Straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps. The ideas became more clear for me, even if it was not so easy the first week, to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were fresh in the team. Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together.

It has been revealed that ‘(Spain) was a complete performance that makes me very proud. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up in this moment.’.

Tuchel, though, has rejected the idea that seeing out the win Madrid was proof that he has learned from his mistakes in Atlanta.

According to recent reports, ‘Not at all, I think we would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11,’ he noted. ‘For me, it was Mexico reloaded (not Argentina). It's one man down, but what can you do? It is their strength to have ball possession, to overload and find the gaps. It just plays totally into their hands and it comes wave after wave. It felt like three hours and thirty minutes!’.

Manchester United reportedly explored several managerial options before eventually appointing Mauricio Pochettino, with former France boss Didier Deschamps among the names sounded out by the Old Trafford hierarchy.

Pochettino ultimately emerged as the preferred choice to replace Michael Carrick, but the search appears to have been broader than first thought.

United were under pressure to make the right appointment after a disastrous start to the season, and senior figures understandably wanted to assess different profiles before committing to another long-term project.

According to talkSPORT, Man United made contact with Deschamps while considering potential successors to Carrick.

The discussions reportedly did not progress very far, with United becoming suspicious that Deschamps may have been using their interest to strengthen his negotiating position elsewhere.

The former France manager had also received a lucrative offer from Saudi Pro League side Al Ahli, reportedly worth around £25million over three years.

In a recent development, united considered other options too, including Antonio Conte and Eddie Howe, while Julian Nagelsmann had previously been sounded out. Ultimately, Pochettino’s Premier League experience, availability and willingness to take the job made him the strongest candidate.

The interesting part of this story is how extensive United’s managerial search appears to have been.

A CaughtOffside report offers a slightly different version of events, claiming United insist Pochettino was the only candidate formally spoken to directly before his appointment.

That does not necessarily contradict reports that Deschamps and others were sounded out through intermediaries, but it does show how fluid the process became behind the scenes.

From United’s perspective, considering multiple candidates was sensible. The club could not afford another rushed managerial decision after years of instability.

Deschamps would have brought enormous international experience, while Conte offered proven Premier League pedigree and Howe represented a safer domestic option.

Pochettino, however, arguably offered the best balance. He already understands English football, has experience managing elite players and has a strong reputation for developing younger squads. He also knows several United-linked players from his time with the United States.

The key question now is whether the club’s careful recruitment process finally delivers stability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for the United States men's national team to win their first Concacaf Gold Cup since 2021, they'll now need to contend with a latest format in the 2027 edition. The tournament will run from June 17 through July 11, with major changes coming to the group stage. It will still include only 16 teams, but instead of those teams being split into four groups of four teams each, they'll now be split into only two eight-team groups. Fifteen of those teams will qualify via the Gold Cup preliminary round and join guest nation Saudi Arabia in the tournament.

That shift has the goal of making the group stage more exciting, as not only does it add an extra game due to each team playing four teams instead of three, but it also allows a chance for chaos, as four teams will go through to the knockouts from each group. While the new game is added, that won't change how the knockouts look, as those will proceed as normal.

Industry observers note that "The Gold Cup is our region's premier men's national team competition, and we are really excited about what this new format will bring to the tournament's Group Stage," said Concacaf president and FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani. "Our fans want to see the best teams in our region compete against each other, and this format will create more opportunities for those matchups to happen earlier in the competition. At the same time, every match will matter, with teams facing a balanced mix of opponents and competing for a place in the knockout rounds. We believe this will make for a more competitive and exciting Gold Cup from the very first match through to the final.".

How matchups are determined is where things get a little confusing, as they will organize the eight teams into ranking bands of two teams each, with a predetermined fixture matrix ensuring that each team plays a balanced schedule of opponents.

This is to prevent a situation where two strong Concacaf sides essentially ensure that others don't have a chance to advance, which could lead to more interesting fixtures in the knockout stages depending on how it goes.

According to recent reports, 🚨🏆 The rumors are confirmed! Gold Cup will have a whole new format in 2027. @FabrizioRomano breaks it down! pic.twitter.com/ydD1ZwbBvK.

For the knockouts, nothing changes from how things used to look, as those four teams advancing from each group will then be placed into a single bracket, with the highest-finishing teams in each group facing off against the lower-finishing teams in the opposite group. There will then be no reseeding as the quarterfinals will determine the semifinal pairings in the road to the championship.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

According to recent reports, as the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, remarked he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Industry observers note that defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Industry observers note that chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

Sources indicate that the problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. But he will also have wondered how United could again have found themselves in such a position after an enterprising first half when they attacked with pace and purpose and looked a very different team to the one that had been ransacked by Como and Bournemouth.

Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

According to recent reports, it left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

It has been revealed that the Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”.

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

It has been revealed that “Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”.

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a massive way,” the United manager noted. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”.

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”.

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”.

We didn’t really get going in the second half. We should have been up in the first half. It was as positive as we could have hoped for. We looked really dangerous.

We found a way of unravelling in the second half. It was a bad goal to concede.

Then there was the penalty and we were right up against it.

I don’t think the heads dropped, there’s no hiding from the fact we haven’t won enough games.

The boys were in a good place in the first half. [Chelsea] made the first blow in the second half and that made the difference.

I’ve not looked at it, I’ve not seen it [the incident that led to Martínez’s red card].

[Do you feel let down by him?] No.

In a recent development, [Do you think the fans who booed them at the end feel let down by the players?] There’s a lot of emotion. We’re a great football club. We want to win football matches. Supporters pay a lot of money and have a lot of commitment to come and see us play. You could see from today that the boys had the game in the right place but things have gone against us in a big way. It unravelled rapidly and there’s a lot of emotion around right now.

We’ve got to move forward. Take the things we believe worked well for us today forward with a bit of confidence. A lot of the good things in the firts half we need to use to move forward.

[Do you expect to be in charge (vs Roma) on Wednesday?] Yes.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

Recent findings suggest that I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

According to recent reports, we know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

If there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UEFA EURO 2028 qualifying draw will take place on December 6: here’s all you need to know, including the Azzurri’s toughest opponents and their ideal group.
  • Italy have secured a place among the seeded teams after finishing third in their Nations League group: 54 countries participate in the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, with 24 spots available for the tournament.
  • There will be five pots: four containing 12 teams each and a fifth with six.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UEFA EURO 2028 qualifying draw will take place on December 6: here’s all you need to know, including the Azzurri’s toughest opponents and their ideal group.

Italy have secured a place among the seeded teams after finishing third in their Nations League group: 54 countries participate in the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, with 24 spots available for the tournament.

There will be five pots: four containing 12 teams each and a fifth with six. Tonight’s matches will determine the final pot allocations.

The draw will result in six groups of five teams and six groups of four. The Azzurri could fall into either category. The 12 group winners and the eight highest-ranked runners-up qualify for EURO 2028.

The other four runners-up and the best-ranked Nations League teams will play for the remaining four spots in the play-offs, but there may be fewer spots available depending on how many host countries qualify.

Teams that qualify for the Nations League semi-finals will be placed in the four-team groups, and those losing in the quarter-finals will go into the five-team groups.

In a recent development, with four Euro 2028 co-hosts, the usual play-off path may change. UEFA could not grant automatic qualification to all four co-hosts, awarding just two spots.

In a recent development, if two hosts qualify through the group stage, the usual format will remain unchanged. If, however, only one qualifies for the tournament, the highest-ranked host nation that failed to qualify will be granted a place, reducing the play-offs to three paths.

If none of the hosts qualify directly, the two highest-ranked will be awarded spots, leaving only two play-off paths to determine the remaining places. However, with England among the co-hosts, this scenario seems highly unlikely.

Italy are in pot 1 alongside Spain, England, France, Belgium, Portugal, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Croatia and Greece, none of which the Azzurri will meet.

The most challenging opponents from Pot 2 seem to be Switzerland, Sweden and Bosnia, not only because each of these three countries has already dealt blows to Italy in recent World Cup qualification campaigns.

Sweden beat the Azzurri in the 2018 World Cup play-off, Switzerland won the qualifying group four years later, and Bosnia beat the Azzurri in the latest World Cup play-off qualifying final this past March.

Slovakia and Scotland seem the toughest opponents from Pot 3.

Gazzetta argues that Italy’s ideal group phase would include Northern Ireland, Romania and San Marino.

Liverpool have joined the growing race for Athletico Paranaense defender Arthur Dias as the Reds continue searching for young centre-backs capable of becoming long-term first-team options.

The 19-year-old has established himself as one of Brazil’s most promising defenders after breaking into Athletico’s senior side in 2025.

His performances have already attracted Tottenham, Barcelona, Bayer Leverkusen and RB Leipzig, but Liverpool are now stepping up their own assessment ahead of future transfer windows.

According to Fussballeuropa, Liverpool have been regularly monitoring Dias and recently sent a scout to watch the Brazilian centre-back in action.

Recent findings suggest that tottenham attempted to sign him during the summer and reportedly offered around €20million, but Athletico Paranaense rejected the proposal. The Brazilian club are now understood to value Dias at approximately €30m, with his contract running until December 2028.

Dias has already accumulated more than 50 senior appearances despite his age and is comfortable playing as the left-sided centre-back. His ability on the ball has also caught the attention of elite clubs, with Barcelona among those to have sent representatives to watch him.

A CaughtOffside report confirms Liverpool’s scouting interest and adds that Dias has completed close to 86 per cent of his passes in Brazil’s Serie A this season.

From Liverpool’s perspective, this is exactly the type of market worth exploring.

Virgil van Dijk is approaching the latter stages of his career, meaning the Reds need to identify potential successors before being forced into an expensive emergency signing.

According to recent reports, dias is left-footed, physically strong and already comfortable progressing possession from defence. Interestingly, he began his youth career as a striker before moving into defence, which may help explain his composure and technical confidence.

Recent findings suggest that there is obviously risk involved in spending €30m on a teenager with no European experience. Adapting from Brazilian football to the Premier League would represent a major challenge.

However, waiting until Dias has proven himself at a Bundesliga or La Liga club could easily double his price.

Liverpool’s strategy should therefore be simple: continue scouting closely and move early if they become convinced.

Tottenham have already discovered that Athletico will not sell cheaply, while Barcelona’s involvement could intensify the competition. If Liverpool genuinely believe Dias can develop into an elite centre-back, €30m may eventually look like the cheaper moment to act.

He faced his fear of heights by skydiving over the Australian coast before tucking into a thick pink liquid, which Ant and Dec dubbed a prawn star martini. According to The Sun, ITV bosses kept Rooney's signing under wraps by giving him a codename, months before the full lineup was declared.

That name has now emerged as 'Wonder', which is a nod to the nickname he used to have in the formative years of his Premier League career.

Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby
