📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Download the Nature Podcast 13 November 2026.

The past year has been... a lot. Record-breaking temperatures, devastating floods and catastrophic wildfires have brought the realities of climate change into sharp focus for people around the world. At the same time, many governments and organisations have scaled back on their climate action.

In a recent development, if you’re anything like me you might be feeling it’s all a bit ‘doom and gloom’. So in this series I decided to face my climate anxiety head on and set out in search of reasons for optimism.

In this first episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about what the data really show and why there are still reasons to hope.

00:00 How climate change feels overwhelming.

04:27 What the data say about renewables.

11:23 Will AI stall climate progress?

21:49 How are the world’s nations doing on climate change?

Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target.

According to recent reports, nature: How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

Nature: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change.

Sources indicate that this episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Daniel Knowler, Akio Jefferson, Lionel Cohen and The Conductor, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Hannah Ritchie, Ketan Joshi and Niklas Höhne for featuring in this episode.

I’m going to be honest with you. I worry a lot.

Industry observers note that I worry about all sorts of things. Money, friends, family, if my voice is weird as you’re listening to it... but there’s one thing I’ve been worried about since I was a teenager in the early 2000s. The climate.

Those anxieties have only gotten worse. In recent years, it has felt like climate action has stalled. In 2024, the world passed the 1.5˚C ‘threshold’ set in Paris for the first time. Shortly thereafter, Donald Trump returned to the White House and on the first day of his Presidency set about reversing climate policies of the previous administration, vowing to promote fossil fuels. In Europe, right-wing politicians have taken aim at climate goals, with the EU weakening previously ambitious environmental policy. All while it’s getting hotter and hotter. In May there were record breaking temperatures in my home of the UK , then in June those records were broken again, twice in the same week in fact, with temperatures in some places across the continent more than ten degrees hotter than they were between 1991-2020. That was the story all over Europe. Without climate change, it’s extremely unlikely Europeans would have had to endure these heatwaves. And globally, scientists of all stripes have expressed doubts that any government has done enough to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

So, it feels like we’re failing on climate, heck, I can even look outside my window and see evidence for that. But what’s weird is that even as climate change is affecting me more, I find it harder to engage with.

As things get worse, I’m having trouble staying optimistic that we, you me and everyone, can do anything about it. And that’s an odd position to be in, as a science journalist. Climate change is one of the biggest stories of our time.

Recent findings suggest that every week, we pick out stories to cover on the podcast. And I always want to report the latest climate science, and I do, but I find it hard. Sometimes it just feels like more bad news at a time when our audience, and I, could do with less. I feel hopeless.

It has been revealed that but is that actually right? Am I justified in that feeling? As the one thing I know about science is often the truth is a bit more complicated than we think. So, while the narrative can feel overwhelming negative, is that really what the data says?

To try and shake myself out of this climate funk, talking to some of the scientists and campaigners on the front lines of climate research, and what I found was a story of: Tipping points….

That has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge.

I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions.

The system is changing at exponential speed.

In a recent development, this is Cooked? a three-part miniseries for Nature, where I try and find out whether we are well… cooked. Is it game over for climate or are there reasons for hope? I’m your host Nick Petrić Howe. And in this first episode, I decided to start with the data, and I had a good idea of who might be able to help me with that.

In a recent development, as a data scientist, I'm biased. And I would say, look at the data to understand for these major problems, where they're coming from, why they're happening, and importantly, what we can do to solve them.

In the past year or so, I’ve found myself struggling with anxiety about the climate. But a couple of years ago a book came out that seemed to fly against what I had assumed was the case, as it stated, backed up with oodles of data, that it isn’t the end of the world. So, I knew I wanted to speak to its author — Hannah Ritchie.

What I wanted to do in that book was, think, twofold.

That’s Hannah, the author of ‘Not the end of the world’ and a data scientist at our World in Data and the University of Oxford.

It has been revealed that one was that I was trying to write it to my former self, who was very, very pessimistic, wasn't sure if there was really a future there for me and present where we are now. And the point is not that these problems are solved in any way, they're still huge problems, but we have started to make progress and there's lots of opportunity for us to make more progress. My point is not that we should be complacent and optimistic that these problems will solve themselves. I think it's to kind of maybe get rid of a bit of the cynicism that there's nothing that we can do and actually no one is doing anything because I don't think that's true. And I think the second kind of motivation for doing that is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and major things that we need to do to solve them?

The book looked at seven huge challenges that humanity faces, including climate change, examining each through the lens of data, to understand the progress we have and haven’t made on them, and what we should do. So I was curious to hear from Hannah about how we were actually doing on climate change.

If you go back 10 years, the world we were sitting in when the world signed the Paris Agreement was that the alternatives to fossil fuels were much more expensive than fossil fuels. For solar and wind were way more expensive. Batteries were extremely expensive. Electric vehicles were basically not on the radar at that point. So it seemed very, very hard to me at the time to see how the world would actually progress on this. What we've seen over the last decade is this huge drop in the costs of these low-carbon energy sources. And that now means that they're cost competitive with fossil fuels, right? So you have the kind of short-term incentive of picking the low-cost solution, now adding up and aligning with the long-term glitch we're trying to solve, which is climate change.

These days renewable energy is very cheap. Let’s take solar energy as an example. Between 2009 and 2025, estimates from the investment firm Lazard suggest solar energy prices have dropped to less than a sixth of what it used to cost on average. This number even includes the continued costs of running solar plants, making them, along with wind, the cheapest form of energy.

It has been revealed that this change has helped Hannah go from pessimistic to optimistic about the future of climate change. It’s not just that the costs have tumbled, more and more this ‘clean’ energy is actually being implemented as well.

In a recent development, we now also see that many countries are now rolling out clean energy at an increasingly fast pace. So it's not like it's just that the cost has dropped. You can actually now start to see that translating into action.

Hannah also thinks that this electrification of the world has other benefits too.

Recent findings suggest that what's really key about that electrification lever, and I think is under appreciated, is how much you gain there in terms of efficiency. You know, it's not just we want to do this because it saves us carbon emissions, which it will if we were powering that through low carbon power, but also you get huge efficiency gains from this. like driving in an electric car uses about a third of the energy of driving in a petrol car, right? So you actually also get rid of lots of this energy waste that we right now have in the system.

Worldwide, adoption rates of electric vehicles are increasing. Around a quarter of every new vehicle sold is electric, and in some countries this rate is much higher. In Norway 97% of new cars sold were electric, while in China 53% were. Now, many people are critical of electrical vehicles for various reasons. Mining of lithium for use in batteries can be very environmentally damaging, for instance. And using public transport is better than having a personal electric vehicle most of the time. But when it comes to their climate credentials, electric cars beat conventional every time.

The world has also been built in many places to favour vehicles and in some areas public transport is not a viable option. So if we want the most people to use the least climate emission causing form of transport, electric vehicles will be part of the mix.

But it’s not just data on clean energy and electrification that gives Hannah hope. She also points to progress that’s been made in making steel and concrete production more climate conscious. They’re maybe a bit less obvious in our day to day lives, as most of us don’t work on substantial construction projects, but these core components of buildings come with big emissions. Cement production, for example, accounted for around 6% of global carbon emissions as of 2024 according to the International Energy Agency.

But this is down from a peak in 2021, due to slowed growth in construction, and is projected to decrease further as improvements are made to the recipe for cement, or alternatives to it entirely are created.

Industry observers note that these solutions haven't been scaled yet. They're at a very, very small level, but I think we still have made progress there and there are actually solutions starting to come online and starting to get cost competitive, but it will take some time for them to build up to a kind of level where you would actually start to see dents in the data.

As Hannah noted, the point of her book and this examination of the data is not to allow us all to pat ourselves on the back and say ‘job’s a good ‘un’. There’s still a lot that we need to do, and in many ways some of these changes aren’t happening fast enough. Rather the point is to not make us feel despondent and hopeless, as that helps nobody.

And there are actually reasons for optimism. Falling prices in renewables, increased electrification and more climate-conscious construction are all starting to make dents in the data according to Hannah.

It has been revealed that so maybe I don't need to be so worried after all. assuming of course that we can keep this up.

Renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is making the rise in emissions less bad.

There's a newly introduced disruptive and energy-intensive technology out there that could stall climate progress. Artificial intelligence.

The level of debate about this technology is massive. It's actually really fascinating because I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

Industry observers note that whenever I open social media these days, I see a lot of scepticism about artificial intelligence. I don’t have to scroll far to come across a video of someone pretending to be a large language model powered chatbot who states silly things while chugging litres of water. But the backlash against the technology is spilling out of social media and pouring into real world legislation. We've seen the first moratoriums on the building of data centres, the facilities that house the infrastructure for AI and other internet services. And often the cited reasons are environmental — water and electricity use.

Recent findings suggest that so that got me wondering, if AI is so energy intensive could it stall climate progress? Especially as many of these data centres are using fossil fuels to meet their energy needs. For the sake of this podcast, I’m just going to focus on energy demands, as that’s what’s more relevant to the climate, and put other environmental concerns to one side for now.

To do so, I wanted to put those memes aside as well and find out what the data actually states. So, I reached out to an expert on data centres and their energy use to go through some of the numbers.

Industry observers note that my name is Ketan Joshi. I'm an independent researcher and analyst, working on energy and data centres and fossil fuel phase-out.

Ketan has been working as energy analyst for many years, but more recently has been focusing on how much energy data centres consume, particularly for artificial intelligence. I wanted to know how a growth in data centres would affect the climate, but he explained to me that that’s a quite a difficult thing to work out.

It has been revealed that we have thousands of projections of data center growth into the near future. But the level of variation that you see in these projections makes me almost want to never use them. and the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway, you know, it'll grow to maybe four to five percent by twenty thirty. I've seen ones that are up to like twenty percent of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway. You know, it'll grow to maybe 4 to 5% by 2030. I've seen ones that are up to like 20% of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind this wild skew of future projections is because there is an inherent assumption about the future of artificial intelligence and the shape and form that it takes in the near future. The way that we tend to formulate projections just falls apart with something like this where there is an inherent uncertainty as to what the technology is, what it's going to be used for, whether it's hype, whether it's real, whether we go for high energy consumption models or low energy consumption models. There's like 10 crisscrossing vectors of uncertainty that make it really, really hard to say what's going to happen.

According to recent reports, the future is, unfortunately, unpredictable. It’s hard to know what AI will look like in 10 years, or even 10 days for that matter. So, it’s tough to fit into our projections of the future and how it may impact the climate. As a result, Ketan likes to focus on the here and now to see what we can understand about the technology. To start, it’s important to note that while AI gets a lot of attention, it right now forms a small part of energy usage. The International Energy Agency, for instance, estimates that data centres use — for everything, not just AI — around 2% of the world’s energy. As Ketan claims, that may grow — perhaps by a lot, perhaps by not so much. It’s part of the uncertainty with the technology.

According to Ketan’s analyses, though, AI and by that, I mean the generative kind that powers chatbots, may be particularly energy intensive.

According to recent reports, something that I've found in the past few weeks actually, having looked at some of the newly introduced newer corporate statements. So for instance, Microsoft analyzed their latest statement, I analyzed Google and Amazon. And all three of those companies are using more energy to earn the same amount of revenue, if that makes sense.

It has been revealed that rather than working towards more efficiency as computing has done in the past, Ketan thinks that companies are using more and more energy to try and make cleverer chatbots, or autonomous AI agents. Google and Microsoft for example, have acknowledged that they’ve increased their energy usage as they build out AI capacity.

Recent findings suggest that one thing to note here is that different use cases of AI have different energy demands. Techniques like Machine Learning which often gets labelled AI, don't use as much energy as generative AI like Large Language Models. And then within generative AI, things like a written response from a chatbot needs a lot less energy than generating an image or a video.

In a recent development, but the concern for the climate is that all this energy needs to come from somewhere. And if there isn’t sufficient renewable energy in place, it will come from fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that figuring out how much data centres may be using fossil fuels, though, is not easy. Ketan explained to me that when companies report their power consumption it’s not quite as simple as them just stating what proportion of renewable energy versus fossil fuels they’ve used. Similarly to carbon offsets, companies can purchase certificates from renewable energy providers and then use them to show that their emissions are lower than they are. Microsoft recently stopped using this method, which has been widely criticised, and in their most recent report there was a large rise in their emissions.

In a recent development, the companies can also have positive effects on renewable energy. With their vast resources they can fund latest wind and solar farms. Microsoft, for example, has declared a $6 billion agreement to build AI infrastructure powered by renewables in Norway. Deals such as these can also then be included in companies’ reports on what kinds of energy they use.

So, untangling all of this is pretty tricky. With that in mind, Ketan explained how energy use has changed in the US, where there’s the most data centres in the world.

Sources indicate that there's a fresh report from the energy information administration, updating on 2025 data. And of course, you know, emissions have gone up. They haven't gone up crazy. Like they haven't gone, you know, it's not like it’s skyrocketing, you know, right angle, but they have gone up and renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is just making the rise in emissions less bad.

Sources indicate that the report Ketan mentioned says that US energy-related CO2 emissions went up by about 2% in 2025. That may not sound like a lot, but it’s against a backdrop of emissions falling, so any rise is a cause for concern for the climate. And like Ketan says, renewable energy adoption has continued apace, so the fact that there were more renewables, but emissions still went up implies that more energy was coming from carbon-emitting fossil fuels.

This is backed up by a report from the Energy Institute, a UK-based professional body that monitors energy use. The report stated that US emissions had increased in 2025 due to higher coal use, and that electricity demand had risen faster than supply driven in part by data centres and artificial intelligence. An independent research firm, the Rhodium group, also identified a rise in carbon emissions in the US and cited a particularly cool winter, more coal use and increased demand in electricity from data centres as reasons.

It has been revealed that of course, data centres could be powered by renewable energy, but building this supply takes time and if we have a sudden increase in energy demand, due to AI for instance, then fossil fuels could be used to plug the gap. Google, for example, has acknowledged that it’s expanding its AI development on a grid that is undersupplied with clean energy, but still remains a large funder of clean energy projects. Google still plans to reduce their emissions, but right now, they’re using more fossil fuel energy.

Recent findings suggest that ketan would like to see more transparency from the tech companies creating AI on its environmental impacts, so it can be scrutinised more easily, along with more regulation from governments. He also thinks that everyone has a role to play deciding on what terms we use this technology.

According to recent reports, ketan is actually optimistic about the future, as it seems that the general public are beginning to understand that they do have the power to demand better from these companies. Environmental, cost and climate concerns are being raised against AI, and politicians are listening — you can look to the growth of moratoriums on data centres to see that. To be clear this isn’t just because of climate, opponents of data centres describe them as being ugly, straining local resources and not providing many tangible benefits to their residents. These are issues that affect people no matter what side of the political divide they sit on. And this bipartisan opposition has meant that politicians have started taking action.

Recent findings suggest that but that touches on another thing I wondered about. What are governments and nations actually doing? Are they meeting the goals they’ve set out for climate? And it’s certainly felt to me like there’s been some backsliding recently — with right-wing politicians taking aim at climate goals.

So, what does the data say about how the nations of the world are doing?

Well, it's better than we used to think 10 years ago, but it's definitely not there where it should be.

It has been revealed that if you’ve ever engaged with climate change, you’ll know that it’s a global issue. The whole world is getting hotter and that affects all of us. Because of that, nations often get together and come up with various pledges on what they’re going to do about that. What comes out of these pledges is ultimately what we, as a global society, are doing about climate change.

And I knew a scientist who keeps close tabs on this, so I gave him a call.

Hello. Niklas Höhne, Upcoming Climate Institute, calling in from Cologne, Germany.

Sources indicate that I met Niklas a few years ago at COP26, the enormous climate conference run by the UN. He co-founded the New Climate Institute, a non-profit that works on climate policy, where he oversees analyses on climate policy. I was there reporting for Nature and I asked him, even back then, if things were hopeless. I remember that he didn’t coddle me or make me despair. He gave a nuanced picture. So, I caught up with him to see where we are now.

It has been revealed that so while 10 years ago we thought global greenhouse gas emissions would rise forever and would lead to a temperature increase of three and half degrees by the end of the century, we now think that with at the moment implemented policies, they will stabilize and decline and then lead to around two and a half degrees by the end of the century. So a full degree better than we thought only 10 years ago. So that's remarkable. That's really good. But it's not enough. The Paris agreement says well below two or in the direction of 1.5 and there we are far away from it. And also, we have to say that in the past years, global greenhouse gas emissions have still increased. So despite all of the efforts, is still more fossil fuels being burned each year and therefore we have more greenhouse gas emissions each year and that means not only are we not stopping climate change, we are fuelling climate change. So, we are accelerating the speed of change each year by adding more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere than we had in the year before.

The main driver of this drop in the projected temperature increase.

is something that Hannah already touched on — the speed of renewable energy production.

Prices are falling and Niklas thinks this may push us to precipice to start some exponential change.

According to recent reports, niklas Höhne: I think the last 10 years we've been surprised each year about the speed of renewable energy, electrification and the transformation that has been started. So, I assume that also next year and the years after we will be positively surprised because the end of that development of the technologies is not there. Yeah. So, prices still decline. New battery technologies are invented. Renewables are incredibly cheap compared to 10 years and are still declining. And what we as humans often underestimate is exponential change. The system is changing at exponential speed. And that means each year more solar is implemented than we thought before or more batteries are implemented, more electric cars. And most of the models, they are still kind of assuming a linear change and underestimate the speed of the transformation. And that's why I think I'm quite optimistic about our future projections that this renewable energy transformation will actually win against the fossil fuels because it's simply exponential change. And that always has to win over a linear trend, which is the one described by the fossil fuels.

You can see a similar exponential change if you look at the history of cars.

According to recent reports, at the turn of the twentieth century there was blight on cities — horses. According to the London Transport museum in 1900 there were 300,000 horses in London. But just 14 years later they’d all but disappeared. This sudden departure of the city’s workhorses helped humanity solve a pretty relevant problem for a climate podcast — pollution.

According to recent reports, horses produced a lot of… waste — you know the kind of waste I'm talking about — that was very literally clogging up streets. The solution, ironically, given the topic of the podcast, was cars. Motorized vehicles had actually been around for a few years in the early 20th Century, but it wasn’t really until 1908 when the Model-T ford came out, the first car affordable to a large number of people, that they really took off. In 1910 there were 8000 cars registered in London, in 1920 there were 190,000, the next year there were 250 000 And as cars took off, streets once clogged with horse manure instead became roads for motorcars.

That may seem like a pretty inevitable change, but if you were a Londoner in 1900, you’d probably wouldn’t have believed that the world could be so different in a few decades.

Industry observers note that perhaps renewable energy will be the same for us. It may seem like we’ll never overcome our addiction to fossil fuels, but as prices tumble, maybe we’re standing on the cliff edge of that exponential change.

According to recent reports, so there are certainly positives for the climate. The speed of the energy transition has taken many experts by surprise. But beyond that, there’s still a long to go. And when it comes to how countries are actually sticking to their climate pledges, it was a bit of a mixed bag.

Recent findings suggest that we regularly look at who is basically the best, which is the best country around the world. And the places one, two, three are always empty. So, no country is doing everything correct. But in each area, you can see quite positive things. We have electric mobility, which is shooting off and was shooting off in Norway because Norway supported it significantly with a lot of money. But now it's basically the better way of doing things. So even countries like Vietnam or Nepal have very high adoption rates for electric cars. They sell more electric cars than conventional vehicles in these countries. And that is remarkable because it demonstrates that this is the most economic way of having individual mobility. Then there's other areas, buildings and industry, which really are a bit behind. And it's very difficult to find really good examples where countries are really doing well. But OK, I think also in buildings and in industry, this idea of electrification is something that will now take off as well. So in buildings, it's heat pumps for heating, which are the fresh normal. So, there's huge opportunity to do more in those areas as well.

Recent findings suggest that you may have noticed that some of the biggest emitters haven’t been mentioned there. And to be honest, they were some of the ones I was most worried about. China and the US.

China is the world’s top emitter according to the International Energy Agency, but it seems that their emissions are finally starting to peak — meaning that the greenhouse gases they emit may be starting to reduce. According to some analyses, they have already peaked. This is likely because they have implemented a huge amount of renewable energy. Last year, China installed more solar capacity than the rest of the world combined, although this boom in installation is slowing down a bit now.

And as Niklas explained to me, China has also been instrumental in producing what the world needs for renewable energy — they’re the leading manufacturer of solar, wind and battery technology. But he did impress on me that that wouldn’t have been possible without the policies of several countries, especially in Europe, promoting renewables and therefore creating the right market conditions for China.

According to recent reports, and then there’s world’s second biggest emitter and the largest historical contributor to climate change. The US. There I was worried about the influence of the most recent administration. Trump’s Team has dealt a severe blow to the world’s ability to tackle climate change, by walking away from Paris Agreement on Climate, for the second time. They also repealed the ‘endangerment finding’ that set out that climate change is a public threat and has been used to enact climate policy. And they have spent billions trying to undo climate projects, giving the companies behind them refunds if they instead invest that money in fossil fuels. These actions, the administration say, would save the United States money by removing excess regulations, lower bills for families and help maintain the US’s leadership. But they are counter to what climate scientists say we should be doing — we need to stop burning fossil fuels and rein in our emissions.

So, I was expecting a pretty negative response from Niklas when I asked about how the US is doing. But he had a few surprises for me.

In a recent development, so for the US as such, it's the second largest emitter and the Trump administration has basically dismantled all climate policies that were there from the federal government in the US. And that means now that the emissions in the US will still continue to decline, but will decline slower.

This first surprise, is that while the actions of the Trump administration will likely increase the emissions that the US will produce, that is against a backdrop of overall decline. Even though there's been a recent uptick in emissions in the past year, the US's emissions have been steadily falling since the early 2000s and that will likely continue. Albeit not as fast as it would if the Trump administration was more pro climate. Ultimately, the economics of clean energy are hard even for the most powerful country in the world to fight against — it’s getting harder and harder to justify the use of fossil fuels when the alternatives are cheaper.

The second surprise was an unexpected way that the current US administration may have unintentionally pushed for a move away from fossil fuels.

In a recent development, which is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. And that created a significant energy crisis with very, very high fossil fuel prices for oil and gas. And that created a push towards energy efficiency and renewable energy. And that effect will be significant. It's very difficult to quantify that right now. But from our point of view, it's very clearly that that will has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge, so to say, and over the tipping point that it will be self-propelling because all the countries that at the moment suffer significantly from fuel shortage is not even a price, a high price is really a shortage that simply have not enough. They will now really, really think about alternatives and have already. So, some countries have already increased their renewable energy targets. China has reduced their oil consumption by 10 to 20%, depending on which source you look at within only 12 months. So, there's significant changes on the way that will reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

According to recent reports, as Niklas mentioned, data on this is hard to get, and this is still an evolving story. Time will tell what the impacts of the war in Iran may be. There have in fact been moves towards and away from renewable energy as a result of surging oil and gas prices — with nations like India and South Korea burning more coal in response to the higher gas prices, while people in the Philippines have taken to installing rooftop solar panels at record rates to avoid the high oil prices. So, a true accounting of the effect of the closure of the strait of Hormuz will take some time. But Niklas’s assessment is backed up by an increased sale of electric vehicles and a record high in solar exports from China, and an analysis by Carbon Brief that suggests that global emissions may fall in 2026. This has led some to wonder whether the war in Iran will be a tipping point for energy — that it will finally end humanity’s addiction to fossil fuels.

Overall, while there are clearly some areas in which the world is behind on its targets, it’s perhaps not as dire as I thought. In terms of renewable energy, adoption is accelerating. True, the current pace won’t be enough to meet our climate goals. We need to stop emitting carbon altogether, and soon if we're to meet the 1.5° target set in Paris, and even then we'll probably have to take some carbon out of the atmosphere. But Niklas, even with all the caveats, was optimistic about the future.

Recent findings suggest that we have all the tools at hand and even now it's economic and the obstacle is not technology, the obstacle is not cost. The obstacle is our inertia in the system and that some lose something and some others gain something. And that is something we as a society really have to overcome.

So, while there’s still a long way to go, there are reasons for optimism. Renewable energy has outperformed many researchers expectations, and continues to do so, in spite of the backlash against it in some quarters. Which, I’ll be honest, does make me feel better. The data tell me that it’s not completely hopeless. When cities were overwhelmed by horses and their waste, cheap motor vehicles changed things in a matter of decades. I’m hopeful that renewable energy can do the same here.

But this is what the data notes, largely about what we’ve already done. I was also curious about what we should do in the future. What are some of the major ideas that can help tackle climate change? That’s next time.

Sources indicate that we could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. But I think having very good affordable substitutes for people to switch to is just really, really crucial.”.

This episode was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. And thanks to Hannah Richie, Ketan Joshi, and Niklas Höhne for speaking to me for this episode.

Mauricio Pochettino's links to Manchester United a natural consequence of USMNT's big swing to hire him

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The patterns of the international match calendar are well known at this point.
  • From the moment Mauricio Pochettino walked into a midtown Manhattan auditorium two years ago to make his opening remarks as the USMNT head coach, his presence has felt temporary to many.
  • In a recent development, the cadence is unusual, since coaches rarely invite reasonable questions about seeking employment elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The patterns of the international match calendar are well known at this point. Players pack their suitcases, board planes, spend a small stretch of days with their compatriots … and in the U.S. men's national team's case, answer questions about their coach landing a latest job.

From the moment Mauricio Pochettino walked into a midtown Manhattan auditorium two years ago to make his opening remarks as the USMNT head coach, his presence has felt temporary to many. It was not just because job security is an increasingly unrealistic concept for soccer coaches, nor was it only down to the fact that Pochettino initially signed a deal that would expire 22 months later. The last two years have been full of reminders that the USMNT job is one of several that could be available to him – he has openly talked about wanting to return to the Premier League, did not deny that his representatives may have met with AC Milan in the weeks before the World Cup and regularly talks about his undying love for Tottenham Hotspur. The latest iteration of a years-long pattern came Tuesday, when reports out of England suggested Pochettino was a top contender for the Manchester United gig, which is not vacant yet but will be once the club finally parts ways with Michael Carrick.

In a recent development, the cadence is unusual, since coaches rarely invite reasonable questions about seeking employment elsewhere. At this stage of Pochettino's tenure with the U.S. team, though, it would be difficult to characterize it as a surprise. It would be equally hard to argue that the pattern does not come with the territory, defender Antonee Robinson acknowledging as much hours after the news broke.

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

"That news kind of got sprung on us, like the rest of the world, I'd say," he noted. "Similar things happened in the past, happened at the World Cup where huge teams lose their manager and they start looking at possible candidates and for us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means we're very lucky to work with a top-level manager but it never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it's the World Cup or whether it's going to be this camp.".

Pochettino's wantaway pattern may be annoying but it reflects the overarching sentiment of his tenure with the USMNT thus far. He is easily the highest-profile coach to take the job and U.S. Soccer is well aware of that. It is why they lined up donors to secure his signature two years ago to make him the federation's highest-paid coach ever, and why there is reportedly a $10 million buyout clause in the newly introduced deal he signed after the World Cup. For the first time in the program's modern history, they hired a coach with genuine international appeal. Even if Robinson should instead spend his time talking about the upcoming Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti, the fact that Pochettino would be courted by others was baked into his appeal.

Industry observers note that "Even when we first met a couple summers ago, there were lots of other people interested in having Mauricio and team join," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson mentioned in May as chatter around the Milan job took center stage in the early days of the USMNT's World Cup preparations. "He had standing offers from other places to come. He wanted to be here. He's a major believer in what we're doing at U.S. Soccer. He's a big believer in soccer in America and he's a big believer in this men's team and so, throughout this entire process, when you have top-class talent, whether it's salespeople, whether it's marketing people or whether it's coaches, other organizations want them and throughout this, Mauricio and team have been incredibly transparent. They've been great partners and are, of course, excited about the summer … There's been a longer list of outreach than what has even been reported and so they've been great about that.".

The key difference here is that he reportedly might be interested in United's offer, according to the Guardian, but the situation remains the same, despite the timing being strange, three months after agreeing a four-year deal. If Pochettino does not end up on United's touchline, his time with the USMNT was never destined to last forever, and U.S. Soccer admitted to it months ago.

Recent findings suggest that "We actually, on a monthly basis, have a succession planning session for all of our coaches across all of our teams and so as a part of that, we have prepares for renewals," Batson mentioned on that May day. "We have plans for interims and we have plans for replacements because you never know what's going to happen. It's a global sport, lots going on and so that's a standard part of us growing up as U.S. Soccer.".

Many might spend the subsequent weeks after Pochettino's hypothetical departure questioning Batson's claim that the Argentine is actually a "significant believer in soccer in America," though the argument is irrelevant as far as the USMNT goes. Pochettino's hire, along with that of U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes a year earlier, was a large statement of intent from U.S. Soccer's leaders like Batson and president Cindy Parlow Cone, who are relatively new to their jobs. Pochettino's exit, therefore, would raise the question of how they continue that vision two years later, especially after outlining an ambitious path for the men's program in the coming years.

High-profile candidates like Pochettino are not exactly easy to come by, as the initial effort to hire him demonstrated. Ex-Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is easily the most notable name on the market but it is entirely unclear what his next coaching move might be, even if that should not discourage U.S. Soccer from reaching out if they have a vacancy. The options thin out from there if they are only to be measured on their flair, though, making it hard to envision a perfect follow-up act to Pochettino in the short term.

There is a theory that U.S. Soccer may be resigned to picking from a locally sourced talent pool, something that is reinforced by a suggestion that Pochettino was a false steward of American soccer. His departure, if it comes in the short term, is not actually an indictment on U.S. Soccer's approach, nor should it encourage the federation to go for the safest pick next. Pochettino's tenure, at least up until this point, has been an example in reaping rewards for a bold strategy, one that should continue long after he is gone.

Pochettino's time with the USMNT has so far been characterized by mixed results, including some low lows that he bears just as much responsibility for as his players. It is not hard to see why he was a good fit for the job, though, and it is not because he makes headlines – his high-intensity, attack-minded style of play actually suited the player pool. The fact that he has coached in a UEFA Champions League final and won a Ligue 1 title with Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappe and Neymar may help with player buy-in, but it would not have papered over the cracks if his version of the USMNT was not actually a decent marriage between his tactical preferences and the players' natural skillsets.

Recent findings suggest that he continues to feel like a good fit in the post-World Cup months, especially as he oversees a generational shift in the player pool. Pochettino's tenure at Spurs, where he initially made a name for himself as a coach, was defined by his trust in young players but as it pertains to the USMNT's up-and-comers specifically, they already seem well-positioned to slot into his tactical set-up. The team's next great prospects are almost all exclusively attackers; Neil Pierre, the Philadelphia Union 19-year-old in the midst of a breakout season, is so far one of the few notable exceptions at center back.

A quote-unquote big name might not be a realistic option for the USMNT if Pochettino leaves now, though he may have theoretically made the gig more attractive to prospective coaches. More importantly, though, U.S. Soccer is now well-positioned to make a hire based on style and specifically an entertaining and effective style that captured the attention of an otherwise uninterested nation during the World Cup. Straying from that, no matter if Pochettino's successor is world renowned or otherwise, would not match the potential of the USMNT's rising stars, nor would it align with U.S. Soccer's own vision.

Liverpool's £123million man is yet to make a major impact for club or country so far this season.

After an ultimately disappointing World Cup in which the French were again by Spain in a major semi-final – following their Euro 2024 exit – long-term manager Didier Deschamps left after 14 years in charge.

Legendary midfielder Zidane succeeded him in the summer and has already led France to the top of their Nations League group – but some of his players may have to go much further to win over their critics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that atlético Madrid has completed the purchase of half of Atlético Fútbol Club, the Guayaquil side that won Ecuador's Serie B in its first season. The deal gives the Spanish club its first affiliate in South America before the Ecuadorian team steps up to Serie A in 2027.

The announcement went up on the Madrid club’s website at 19:00 on 13 November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the move had been signalled earlier in the year. On Friday 20 February 2026, Atlético mentioned it would share sporting, institutional and commercial expertise with Atlético FC and might take a stake in the following months, El Comercio reported.

Regarded as Ecuador’s largest non-profit organisation, the Junta de Beneficencia de Guayaquil operates in all 24 of the country’s provinces.

Sources indicate that the club’s route into Serie B was unusual. It took over the place of Atlético Vinotinto, which could not use it because its affiliate Vinotinto FC had been relegated. The team also changed its name from Atlético JBG to Atlético FC.

Sources indicate that promotion came on 15 October 2026 with a 1-0 win over Independiente Juniors. Fidel Martínez scored the goal. A week later, on Thursday 22 October, a 2-2 draw against Cuenca Juniors at the Estadio Alejandro Serrano sealed the title. That match was the ninth round of the promotion hexagonal.

Across the campaign the side scored 39 goals and conceded 21. It became the 37th different club to win Ecuador’s Serie B. The team is coached by Carlos Santamarina, who comes from Atlético’s academy.

In a recent development, the promotion also reshapes the city’s football map. Guayaquil will have four clubs in the 2027 Serie A: Atlético FC, Barcelona SC, Emelec and Guayaquil City.

Mexico and Canada already host clubs in the Madrid side’s network of linked teams, through Atlético de San Luis and Atlético Ottawa.

It has been revealed that the investment builds on years of groundwork in Ecuador. Atlético and the Junta signed their original strategic agreement on Monday 24 July 2023 at the charity’s sports complex. Under that deal, the club’s academy would apply its coaching model to the Junta’s football division. At the time, that division served 2,500 children from vulnerable backgrounds.

Sources indicate that in June 2026 the club put the number of young players at more than 14,000. That same month, chief executive Miguel Ángel Gil Marín visited the academy’s Guayaquil base. With the Junta’s delegation, he watched an Atlético FC match and greeted Santamarina.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

In a recent development, A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

It has been revealed that “There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

Sources indicate that the result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

Sources indicate that A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

According to recent reports, referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

In a recent development, it might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola stated Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

Recent findings suggest that “That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

In a recent development, arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

According to recent reports, “That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta stated. And that was indisputable.

Recent findings suggest that even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Industry observers note that arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

According to recent reports, in fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

In a recent development, there was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It has been revealed that it would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

It has been revealed that whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. Team news should come through at 3.15pm.
